title: If you are reading this please go to bed
cover-description: Sometimes, the most productive thing you can do is get some rest.
content:
If you're reading this, please go to sleep.

For a long time, I avoided sleep because I thought I needed to stay awake all night to finish an assignment or project. If I did not finish it that same night, I felt unproductive, even after spending the entire day working. I did this for years. Not every night, of course, but often enough that I eventually realized it was hurting me more than I understood.

My goal here is simple. I want to convince you that it is okay to put down your pen, close your laptop, and continue tomorrow.

I am close to finishing my Computer Science degree at Cal State Bakersfield. I have been trying to enter software engineering during a difficult job market, and I often felt that students from schools without structured recruiting had to work even harder. In my town, agriculture is the biggest industry. I worried that I would have to do more if I wanted to land a job in Silicon Valley or somewhere else in the field.

Early on, I realized my degree alone was not going to save me. I would need to work outside of class if I wanted one of those roles. That meant practicing data structures and algorithms, preparing for interviews, learning system design, and building personal projects.

Some days, school assignments and projects took up my entire day, from 8 a.m. until 9:30 or 10 p.m. At the end of those days, if I did not spend more time practicing LeetCode, reading LearnCpp, or watching interview guides, I felt like I had wasted the day.

So what did I do? I stayed awake. I tried to learn every LeetCode pattern and worked on personal projects. Even when I knew a project probably would not be the deciding factor in whether I earned the six-figure salary I wanted, I kept going.

Eventually, I started falling asleep in class almost every other day. I was missing important material that I would later have to relearn for quizzes and exams. I would fall asleep on the couch in the student lounge, wake up, remember that I had work to do, and then fall asleep again a few minutes later.

That cycle created even more work. I had to spend extra hours catching up on lectures and assignments. I still considered those hours unproductive because they were not going toward LeetCode, system design, or STAR interview responses.

I could not keep spending entire days stressed about catching up on classwork. I needed to let my brain rest so I could come back the next day ready to work. Otherwise, I would spend ten hours trying to learn material from six or seven hours of lectures that I had been too tired to understand.

I needed a solution. If only the answer had been obvious.

It was sleep.

At first, it was hard to stop working and come back to it the next day. I felt anxious that I would forget what I was learning or that something bad would happen because I had stopped. But when I returned to the work the next morning, it was usually easier to finish. The lessons were easier to follow. The concepts made more sense. My problem-solving felt sharper.

That probably sounds like common sense. However, once you get stuck in that cycle, common sense is not always enough to change your behavior.

I am not telling you to take every weekend off, put everything off, and expect good results. I am saying there is a point where pushing harder creates more work instead of helping you make progress.

Give yourself enough time between starting an assignment and its deadline. Take breaks. Pay attention to when another hour of work stops being useful.

You should not destroy your health for the work that is supposed to help you build a life you enjoy. Try not to build up a sleep debt before you realize how much it is costing you.

As I write this, I still have two projects to catch up on, interview prep to do, classes to study for, and a personal life to balance. But tonight, I think it is best to leave you with a goodnight.

I will see you tomorrow.

Best,
Fernando
